analysis.one_liner: Bans discrimination based on sexual orientation in jobs, housing, credit, services, and public facilities.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 76 cosponsors but never got a committee vote or a floor vote, dying in House subcommittees when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal to treat someone differently because they are gay, lesbian, or perceived to be — in hiring, at school, when getting a loan, renting an apartment, buying goods or services, using public facilities, or in any program that receives federal money. It was introduced in January 1993 and sent to two House committees. It never got a hearing that led to a vote, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Gay, lesbian, and bisexual Americans, and people perceived to be LGBT, who could be fired, denied housing, refused credit, or turned away from businesses and public facilities because of their sexual orientation. The bill would give them the same kind of legal protection that federal civil rights laws provide for race, religion, and sex.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to discriminate based on actual or perceived sexual orientation in employment, education, credit, and housing.
Extends the ban to the sale or use of goods and services, public facilities, and any federally assisted program, giving broad protection beyond just the workplace.
Draws protection in the same style as existing federal civil rights law, covering perception as well as actual orientation.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, landlords, lenders, and businesses open to the public would carry the cost of complying: changing policies, and facing lawsuits if they discriminate. There is no significant public spending in the bill as introduced.

drawbacks.text: The bill covers nearly every kind of commerce, including the sale of goods and services and public facilities — far broader than later workplace-only proposals — which would mean compliance burdens and litigation exposure for many small businesses, not just large employers.

As introduced, the bill states the prohibition but does not spell out detailed enforcement machinery or exemptions, including for religious organizations, leaving major design questions unresolved that critics would have pressed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: federal legal protection for a group that, in 1993, could be fired or denied housing with no national law to appeal to. The costs are diffuse compliance and litigation burdens spread across employers and businesses, which is the normal cost of any nondiscrimination law. The bill's biggest weakness was not its goal but its brevity — the introduced version did not resolve how it would be enforced or where exemptions would fall, which is exactly the kind of thing committee work is supposed to fix. Instead, it got no committee action at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Judiciary and Education and Labor committees, then parked in their civil rights subcommittees, and neither committee ever advanced it to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 5, 1993, and referred jointly to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Education and Labor Committee.
In February 1993 it was referred to subcommittees in both committees — Civil and Constitutional Rights in Judiciary, and Select Education and Civil Rights in Education and Labor — where it sat.
It gathered 76 cosponsors, including 72 Democrats, 3 Republicans, and 1 Independent.

The only further action in the entire two-year Congress was the sponsor's introductory remarks printed in the Congressional Record in April 1994; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, landlords, lenders, and businesses that wanted to keep the legal ability to consider sexual orientation in hiring, housing, credit, and service — they kept that ability. LGBT Americans remained without federal protection until much later.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Businesses free to discriminate; no federal protection

for.name: Henry A. Waxman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and kept it on the record with introductory remarks in 1994.

for.name: Barney Frank, Gerry Studds, and other original cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Joined as original sponsors alongside Waxman when the bill was introduced.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including later additions like Pelosi, Schumer, and Sanders.

against.role: Committee of primary referral (Chair Jack Brooks, D-TX)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never brought it to a committee vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic — 72 Democrats to 3 Republicans and 1 Independent — and the bill died in committees controlled by the Democratic majority.

industries.note: The bill would have exposed employers to legal claims for firing or refusing to hire people based on sexual orientation. Their interest in avoiding that liability ran against workers' protection.

industries.industry: Housing providers, lenders, and public-facing businesses
industries.note: Landlords, creditors, and shops open to the public would have faced the same prohibition in housing, credit, and services, with new compliance duties and litigation risk.
